models.summary: An insurance pricing model built on multiscale geographically weighted regression. Ninety-six ERA5-Land climate variables are standardized and cut by principal component analysis to four components that keep 42.1, 16.6, 13.7, and 10.6 percent of the variance. Grid climate is moved onto event coordinates by bivariate spline interpolation, and an event is flagged when an interpolated variable crosses a climatic threshold. The payout at a location is an intercept plus the four components plus the probability of an extreme event, each with its own location-specific coefficient. The premium is a base times one plus a scaled risk score, times a humanitarian adjustment coefficient of the local socio-economic factors, times a profitability factor equal to the historical payout ratio plus a target margin. The two adjustment factors are then optimized to balance humanitarian impact against profitability, with the solver left unnamed. An improved grey model GM(1,1) is fitted to the accumulated series by least squares and inverted to forecast 2024 to 2034. California is read as high risk, rising from 2013.94 to 3100.54, Texas as medium, and Nebraska as low, though the prose later calls Nebraska medium too.

models.summary: Two protection layers built on the payout regression. Community administrators enter as one more covariate, a protection level with its own location-specific coefficient. Risk is one minus the ratio of the community's capacity to the maximum capacity, cost is a base plus a coefficient times the protection level times a unit cost, and the loss sums risk plus a weighted cost over locations. The three quantities are solved with scipy and read off Figure 5 as a positive correlation, with about 70 percent protection against about 30 percent cost. Property owners are handled by an improved entropy weight method on twelve socio-economic indicators: min-max normalization, entropy, weights, a weighted index, and a linear map from that index to the humanitarian coefficient, trained on historical premiums. Table 4 prints weights of 0.375, 0.250, 0.250, and 0.125, while the advice quotes 0.444, 0.389, and 0.278.

models.summary: A preservation layer that reuses the payout regression on buildings. A significance score weights cultural importance at 0.4, historical at 0.3, economic at 0.2, and community at 0.1, after min-max normalization. The Ernest Hemingway House scores high on culture and low on community; the Illinois State Capitol scores high on history and low on economics. The required protection level, in the same three tiers as the insurance risk, is then regressed on building size, age, material cost, and structural complexity, plus the coordinates. For the Statue of Liberty the coefficients run 0.7 to 1.0 for size, 0.5 to 0.7 for age, 0.5 to 1.0 for material cost, 0.5 to 1.0 for structural complexity, and 0.7 to 1.0 for the coordinates, which the paper reads as the top protection tier at about 2.5 million dollars a year.
